title: How to Cure the EBSA Epidemic
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles tackles Emotionally Based School Avoidance (EBSA), the anxiety-driven pattern behind rising persistent and severe absence in English schools. He admits up front that we do not really know what works in mainstream settings, because few local authority guidelines have been measured for impact and the best case studies come from alternative provision. Rather than prescribe a fix, he used NotebookLM deep research over 40-plus sources to generate five candidate interventions and offers leaders a structured team vote (75 percent average to adopt, with a re-vote when a doubter objects) to decide which to try. The five options are graduated low-demand reintegration, relational culture-based models, autism-specific sensory adjustments, collaborative modular CBT, and the Assess-Plan-Do-Review cycle. He then summarises whole-school and targeted adjustments, gives national absence statistics, and sets out the Kearney and Silverman four-function model of causes. The piece is candid that much guidance rests on practitioner consensus rather than controlled trials, and that punitive fines and forced attendance appear to worsen the problem.
points: Salles argues the honest starting point is that evidence for mainstream EBSA interventions is thin, so leaders should treat any plan as a hypothesis to monitor rather than a proven fix.

His blind-vote method (individual scores, 75 percent threshold, a re-vote when someone scores below 70 percent, and a checklist of early warning signs for doubters) is a reusable way for a team to adopt or drop interventions.

Graduated reintegration works through an anxiety hierarchy, tiny early steps, a safe space, and explicit permission to step back without it counting as failure, whereas forcing full-time attendance tends to cause relapse.

For autistic students the avoidance is often sensory pain and masking exhaustion, so sensory audits, low-demand safe spaces, predictability and avoiding over-scaffolding matter more than anxiety-focused CBT.
The Assess-Plan-Do-Review cycle with reviews every 4 to 6 weeks underpins every successful approach and is what demonstrates a systematic response to inspectors.
quotes: Every Local Authority has a set of guidelines about what you should be doing but it seems that almost no one has gone out to actually measure the impact of any of those things.
Tell your team that any vote which averages 75% or more will be carried - you will implement that thing.

This approach avoids the “too much, too soon” trap, replacing forced full-time attendance with a highly structured, incremental return based on the child’s anxiety tolerance. Forcing immediate full attendance consistently causes relapse.

For neurodivergent students, traditional anxiety interventions (like Cognitive Behavioural Therapy) often fail because their avoidance is driven by genuine sensory pain, cognitive overload, and the exhaustion of “masking,” rather than irrational phobias.
Review: Hold review meetings every 4 to 6 weeks to evaluate progress. Ask what has gone well, what has failed, and adjust the plan accordingly.
Severe absence has seen a massive 193% increase (a near-tripling) since the pandemic. In 2018/19, only 0.81% to 0.85% (around 57,000 pupils) were severely absent.
Mainstream schools are advised to move away from punitive attendance cultures and instead foster environments rooted in psychological safety and belonging.
Researchers warn that varying school attendance problems are often grouped under loose labels without clinical precision.
